WalkthroughText: When analyzing code informally, one of the most useful skills is tracking how many times a particular statement runs, especially inside loops. Rather than just reading code and guessing, you can attach an invisible counter to the statement you care about and increase it by one every single time that statement's line actually executes. This counter overlay sits alongside your normal variable tracking in the trace table, letting you visually confirm loop bounds, catch off-by-one errors, and verify nested loop totals by watching the counter tick up step by step as you walk through the code exactly as the computer would.

PracticeItems.Explanation: The loop variable i starts at 0 and runs while i < 5, so i takes on the values 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 — that is 5 iterations. Each iteration executes the body once, so the assignment line runs exactly 5 times. Choosing 4 would happen if you forgot that i=0 is a valid iteration; choosing 6 would happen if you mistakenly included i=5, which fails the condition and stops the loop.

For each of the 3 values of i (0,1,2), the inner loop runs completely through j = 0,1,2,3, which is 4 iterations. Since the inner loop restarts fully for every outer iteration, the total executions are 3 times 4 = 12. Answering 7 would be adding the loop bounds instead of multiplying the number of iterations, which is a common but incorrect shortcut.

Tracing the value of x each iteration: start x=10 (10>0, execute, x becomes 7), x=7 (execute, x becomes 4), x=4 (execute, x becomes 1), x=1 (execute, x becomes -2). Now x=-2, which is not greater than 0, so the loop stops. That is 4 executions total. Choosing 3 would undercount by stopping one iteration too early, before x actually drops to a non-positive value.

WalkthroughSteps.Caption: Here is our code: a loop that counts from i = 0 while i is less than 3, printing a message each time. We want to know exactly how many times the print statement executes, so we'll attach a counter overlay to that line.
We check the loop condition: is i less than 3? Since i is 0, this is true, so we enter the loop body.
The print statement executes. Our counter overlay on that line increases from 0 to 1 — this is the first execution.
Now i increments from 0 to 1, and we loop back to check the condition again.
i is 1, still less than 3, so the condition is true again. The print statement runs a second time, and our counter overlay ticks up to 2.
i increments to 2, and the loop checks the condition once more: is 2 less than 3? Yes, true — so we execute the body a third time, and the counter overlay rises to 3.

Finally i increments to 3. Now the condition i less than 3 is false, so the loop stops without executing the body again. Our counter overlay stayed at 3, which is exactly the number of times the print line ran — matching the 3 values 0, 1, and 2 that i took on.
